screens.heading: The oldest trick in a new disguise

teacher.say: Welcome! Let's start with the one idea that everything else builds on.

body: Phishing is a type of fraud in which an attacker pretends to be someone you trust, in order to make you hand over information, money or access.
The name echoes fishing. The attacker casts a believable bait, such as a delivery notice, a bank alert or a message from your manager, and waits for someone to bite.
Phishing is not a software flaw. It is a conversation, and the target is a person.
screens.key_takeaway: Phishing attacks people, not computers. The weak point is trust.

screens.heading: Same goal, different channels

teacher.say: Tap each channel on the diagram. The names matter, because they tell you what to expect.

body: The goal is always the same, but the channel and the amount of effort change.

points.label: Email phishing
points.text: Mass messages posing as banks, couriers or popular services. Cheap to send and aimed at everyone.

points.label: Spear phishing
points.text: A message written for one person, using real details such as your name, role or a project you work on.

points.label: Whaling
points.text: Spear phishing aimed at senior leaders, or at the people who can move money for them.

points.label: Smishing
points.text: Phishing by SMS or chat app, usually a parcel problem, an unpaid fee or a security alert.

points.label: Vishing
points.text: Phishing by phone call, often a caller claiming to be from your bank, IT support or a government office.

points.label: Quishing
points.text: Phishing through QR codes on posters, emails or parking meters. The code hides the address it leads to.

screens.key_takeaway: Phishing is not only email. Any channel that reaches you can carry it.

screens.heading: Anatomy of an attack

teacher.say: Attacks are rarely random. Watch how much happens before you ever see the message.

body: Most successful attacks follow four steps. Knowing them helps you spot where you can break the chain.

points.label: 1. Research
points.text: The attacker collects names, roles, suppliers and brands from company websites and social media.

points.label: 2. Bait
points.text: A message is built to look routine and to trigger an emotion such as worry, curiosity or a wish to help.

points.label: 3. Action
points.text: The victim clicks, opens a file, signs in, pays or replies. This is the only step the attacker cannot do alone.

points.label: 4. Payoff
points.text: Stolen credentials are used or sold, malware is installed, or money moves to the attacker.

example.title: A realistic example
example.text: A finance employee is found on a professional networking site. The attacker learns the name of a regular supplier and sends an email about a changed bank account. One reply later, a genuine payment goes to the attacker.

screens.key_takeaway: The victim's action is step three. That is where you can stop the attack.

screens.heading: Why attackers keep choosing it

teacher.say: Understanding the attacker's motivation makes you much harder to fool.

body: Phishing is cheap, and one message can reach thousands of people. Even a tiny success rate pays for itself.
It also walks around technical defences. A firewall cannot block a person who chooses to type a password into a fake page.
One stolen password can be enough. Your email account can reset the passwords of almost every other account you own, so an attacker who controls it controls much more.
screens.key_takeaway: A single stolen password can unlock your email, and your email can reset almost everything else.
